The oral mucocele/ranula is another condition that has been linked to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. However, it is essential to note that there are some exceptions.

In general, HIV-positive individuals may be at an increased risk of developing oral mucoceles or ranulas due to the compromised immune system and potential opportunistic infections. This condition can manifest as a localized lesion on the tongue, floor of the mouth, or inside the cheeks.

The exact clinical picture of oral mucoceles/ranulas in HIV-positive patients differs from what is observed in HIV-negative individuals. The authors suggest that this may be due to the distinct immunological and pathological profiles of the two groups.

It's essential for healthcare providers to consider the possibility of an HIV-related salivary gland disease when evaluating patients with oral mucoceles or ranulas, especially if they are suspected to have HIV infection.
